National income is the total money value of all goods and services produced by a country within a given period, usually one year. It measures the economic performance of a nation. It can be looked at in three ways that should give the same total: the output (product) approach, the income approach, and the expenditure approach. Key related terms include Gross Domestic Product (GDP), Gross National Product (GNP) and Net National Product (NNP). WAEC frequently tests the meaning and methods of measuring national income.

GDP (Gross Domestic Product) is the total value of all goods and services produced within a country's borders in a year, regardless of who produces them (citizens or foreigners). GNP (Gross National Product) is the total value of goods and services produced by a country's citizens in a year, whether at home or abroad. The link is: GNP = GDP + net income from abroad (income earned by citizens abroad minus income earned by foreigners within the country). So GDP is about location, while GNP is about ownership/nationality.

Why is national income used to measure standard of living?

National income, especially per capita income (national income divided by population), is used to estimate the average standard of living, because a higher income per person usually means people can afford more goods and services. However, it is not a perfect measure for several reasons: (1) it ignores how income is distributed, so a few rich people can raise the average while many remain poor; (2) it does not show the kinds of goods produced (more weapons does not improve welfare); and (3) it ignores leisure, environmental damage and the informal sector. So national income should be used alongside other indicators when judging welfare.
